title: Hall-effect thruster channel-wall erosion at high power
bottleneck: Hall thrusters accelerate ions with crossed electric and magnetic fields, but the same plasma bombards the discharge channel walls, sputtering material away. At higher voltages the erosion rate climbs sharply; once the wall wears through, the magnetic circuit is exposed and the thruster fails. NASA's 50-kW-class nested Hall thruster program states the technology cannot currently be used on deep-space missions because of lifetime issues, with erosion the main failure mechanism.
why_it_blocks: Efficient electric propulsion enables cargo pre-positioning and fast deep-space transits; without thrusters surviving tens of thousands of hours, long missions must carry excessive redundancy or accept degraded performance.
current_state: Magnetically shielded designs reshape the field so plasma potential near the walls stays high, dramatically reducing erosion. A 50-kW-class shielded thruster is in fabrication and testing; long-life validation is ongoing.
